entries.text: Page I See
SIEWAL VY ES? aS
Side A: Interview with Herman Larson (age 98 years at the time) by Dennis Signalness and Leroy Hanson circa 198 -
transcribed from tapes: [DS used below since unable to tell whether DS ortr was asking eee

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Can you tell me how the traps were designed?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Well, the traps were brush stuck down in the mud, just as thick as they possibly could, leaning down wind. Then the main trap was .... The fish would follow the stream and get into the main trap. There was a wing on each side.... if there was a channel coming here, there would be a wing on each side leading into the trap. The wings were downstream, so the trap ...when the fish come up the stream, they'd find the wings and go into the trap and they could raise the trap up to get the fish out.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: And it was probably made of brush too?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: The trap itself was made of sticks .

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: I mean the part that would raise up?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: That was made out of sticks, and it was a little like a basket.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Like a basket, uh huh. And that would probably be right in the center part of the channel, the deepest part...

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Yeah, the deepest part of the channel, that's where it would be.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Do you recall traps along the bay? On the different little tributaries to the bay?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Yes, they trapped up North Inlet, they trapped there at Goose Point, the channel that comes out from Goose Point, at Lone Rock, and there were traps at Kentuck Inlet. Las o bE exe

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Where was the trap at Kentuck?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Well, it was out pretty well where the old Hardy mine was, you know where the old Hardy mine was?

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Yes, just over the ridge from my place .

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Out this way. And then up at Cooston, there was a big trap up there. On the inside channel that comes up Coos River. That was a real big trap.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: The people that would tend these traps, that built the traps - where would they live?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Man the traps? They were generally camping. They didn't live [there]. They'd come from all over, and camp there during fishing season.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Were there any permanent camps here on the bay or were they constantly moving along?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: That's before my time. I don't know anything about that.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Getting off the fishing end of it, do you recall any bull team camps along this upper bay?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Certainly, I worked in them.
We've got pictures of them.

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: I used to break oxen for leaders.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Mrs. Morgan showed us a picture the other night of her husband [should be of her father] with his bull team. It is in the new book that Mrs. Mahaffey has just published. Where would those camp sites be?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: They were all over. There's camp sites at Glasgow. There's campsites all up Coos River. You mean the bull teams?

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Yes

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: They were all over the country.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Was there one at Glasgow?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Well, certainly. Peter Durgan and Ron Noble had a camp there. They logged up 160 acres there at Glasgow. I worked there. 160 acres for a town site. Durgan and Ron Noble sold logs to ... Simpson. They got 150 dollars an acre for it too. They logged the land off... They got the timber for nothing. They logged that off and dumped the logs off in the gulches and burnt it.... that's before they ever started the town site there.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Do you recall where the logs came into the bay at Glasgow?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: They came in just about where the ferry landing was. There was another dump - there used to was - towards Kentuck. They had two dumps there.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Do you know of any Indian campsites along this part of the bay - between here and say the sand hills on the east side of the bay?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: The biggest camp site was Old Town

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: AT Old Town?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Yeah, at the east of the bridge, that goes across the bay. That was the biggest Indian camp there. Then there was camp at the edge of Larson Inlet. And there was a camp at Goose Point.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Is that where Anderson's place is?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Yeah, Goose Point and there was a camp at Glasgow too. There was a camp up where Peterson's ok! place - Hollow Stump,

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: and there was a camp at Lone Rock. That's a camp up Coos River, and, of course south of the bay, South Slough they had lots of camps out there.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: These camps, would there be many people to a camp, or just be a family maybe?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: No, big crowds of people.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Do you know approximately where the campsite would be in the Glasgow area? We ask about this because we've lived around Glasgow and we're kind of familiar.

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: The camp would be just a little east of the old ferry landing and then there was a camp right just around the point where the highways cross. There was Indians in there. On the right hand side of the highway, right in the cove there.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Do you recall of any old sailing ship wrecks that were on the upper bay here, that were pulled in, or run aground??

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Well,. my father came here in '62. He was wrecked on Coos Bay bar. He stayed here about 18 months. He worked for old man Simpson and also he worked up there for push.... at Marshfield. He got a ship and went back to San Francisco and went back to Norway and got married. Around the horn... He stayed in Norway a short time, not very long. He came back to San Francisco... when they came back from San Francisco [Norway], they came over the Isthmus of Panama, and came to San Francisco, and stayed there, oh about a year. My oldest sister was born in San Francisco. He didn't stay there very long, and he came up to Coos Bay. He stopped there at the Golden Eagle Hotel in Empire. He knew those old people had had a hotel there before he went home to Norway. So he stopped there, and he got a job down at south inlet for a fellow by the name of Charlie Brown. He worked there in the camp and did the cooking. They stayed there for almost a year, then they moved up to Larson Inlet. There was an old gentleman there by the name of Charlie Holdrig[?]. He took up a claim up Larson Inlet. He told my father he didn't think he'd prove up on it, so he told my father to take it. Well, my father stayed a very short time. And there's where I was born, right where the bridge crossed, through the Erickson place. He didn't stay there long. When the big fire come, why, that wiped us out. He took us down to the sand dunes. That was in '68 and took the sand ... And then we went back and built another house there at the Erickson place, and stayed there a very short time, and took the place up through there.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: That's sure interesting. This fire, did it wipe out any other homesteaders?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Well, nobody much around, only a sawmill, al] they did was trapping and hunting for hide and so forth. No farms, not much of anything. And that fire came down, it was about 12 - 14 miles wide, and 16 - 18 miles long. It came down from Schofield Creek. It came down through, between North Haynes Inlet and Larson Inlet, and she spread out to the coast, and up over as far as Golden x Falls. And stopped there, just at the mouth of Larson Inlet, and on to Kentuck Inlet and over to Coos River.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Now that we're talking about the fire, reminds me of the story that it was that fire that killed the oysters. Did you ever hear that?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Nothin' to it. That's all bunk. That's what an Indian told me.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Well, he ought to know. Well, have you ever heard the story of the Indians burying their canoes or hiding their canoes up by Hauser when they were sent up to the reservation?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Hiding their canoes? I never heard of that. Maybe they did, but I didn't know of it.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: We heard that they planned to come back and they wanted to hide canoes so they'd have them when they came back again. They buried them in the sand, but J can't recall where I'd heard it now.

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: That might be true, I don't know. .. I remember when they came back the second time, and gathered them up. There was quite a few they didn't get [?]...... at the last minute, the first time. The second time when they came back, why I remember that.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: In your lifetime, how did the Indian live? Did they have... What kind of protection did they have for a house? They didn't have saw-milled sawn boards did they?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: No, they didn't have that. Tulles principally. These tulles, they'd have them together just like mats. That's what they slept on too. You know those - you might call them bull rushes, I don't know.... [other voices ]

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: They have cattails on the end of them, a round reed. They probably would weave those together with grasses to make a mat?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Yes, they just ...[2] reeds with a cord right through them so they'd be close like that. That's principally what they had for protection.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: I know several years ago we the found remains of an Indian home or lodge down on the Sixes River. It was dug down into the sand, probably about 4 feet, and they had up upright planks, not sawn planks, but split planks. We couldn't tell how they got into it, but see the remains of planks about that high sticking up.

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: I wouldn't know anything about that.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Maybe they used bark or something for the roof.

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Perhaps so.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Have you ever seen an Indian burial? Don't I remember something about an Indian burial on that other tape?
Yeah, on that other tape told about helping bury their Indian woman?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Oh yeah.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: I thought that would be interesting to hear that again..

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Well, I have to tell ya that anyhow. I had a workshop up on the ranch over the horse stable. There was an old fellow by the name of Lyman. He lived down on the mouth of Larson Slough. He was a little old fellow. One day he came up morning. about 10 or 11 o'clock I think it was. He told me his tootsum had died.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: What did he call it?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Tootsum.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Was that her name?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: No, that's his wife, died. He asked me to make a mem-a-loose box - a coffin.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Oh, that's pretty interesting.

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: And so, I had some light lumber there and I started to make it and I made the coffin all right. The next morning, oh it was really something to look on. So I put the coffin in the boat and pulled down to the mouth of the slough, and I carried the coffin up on the hill where the old shack was. He was very , oh, he hardly could do anything at all. So asked him where I should dig the grave. He took me outside about 40 feet from his shack there and he looked east and west and so forth. And he marked out where I should dig the grave. Oh, it was nothing but clay. I brought a shovel with me. So I took it down. I asked him how deep I should dig it. And he ... only hip room here.... Now he was a short man, why it wasn't very deep. So I dug it that deep. Then after I just dug then, I went into the house to put the body into the coffin. So, I put the old body in the coffin and then there was an old squaw there, she kept piling stuff in the coffin, and I couldn't get the lid on, to nail the lid down - she had so much stuff in there.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: What was she putting in there Herman?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Oh clothes, and everything you know. So finally, J got by[?] and nailed the lid down and nailed it pat. Then I was stuck. I couldn't carry it, so I went down to the boat and got a rope and I drug the coffin out. That's the end of the story.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Oh for goodness sake.
How'd you get it in the hole?

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: How'd you get it lowered down in the hole?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Oh, I just slid it right down. It had boards. Had a board and slid it in the hole and pulled the board.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: What kind of a shack did these Indians live in?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Oh, just old boards. That they'd pick up on the beach.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: And he lived up on a hill?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Yes, just a house, right on, built on the top of the grade now, that house up there. And then I helped bury another one on the other point, east of there. There's a house over there too. Old Henry Miller helped me bury that one. Did you know Henry Miller?

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: No, I heard mea Rowe pagaer YK)

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: He used to own "Phoebe Reher's [?] place”. :

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Oh, I've heard the name. Course, he was long before my time. Well, this second burial ground - that would be on the Haynes , over on the north side of Haynes?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: No, It'd be east of the one right up Larson Inlet there. There's a house up there too.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Oh, yes. By where Howard Hendrick lives?
Howard Hendrick lives on the ... first one. The other one is around the corner. I don't know who lives there. Johnson..

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: How did these old people get out and scrounge enough to eat Herman? Did they live off of clams, do you think?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Well, they was for a while. They could help themselves. They got so bad that they couldn't do anything. My father went to the County Court and told the County about these poor Indians and so he got 5 dollars a month on this side of the bay. He took that to the old country store at North Bend and he told them not to give them nothing but provisions - not no nonsense. So that went along for quite a long time. So that's the only thing... My father ...pigs ..like that got from father.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Well, that was sure nice.

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: So, they got 5 dollars a month from the County .

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Do you recall what kind of canoes or dug-outs they had Herman? Were they out of logs? Or were they

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Generally out of red cedar. Most of them were out of red cedar. Some out of white cedar.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Have you ever witnessed a canoe or dug-out being built?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Well, yes. I haven't seen all of it. They would burn a lot of it. They'd burn a lot of it I've seen it after they ‘d fixed it. They'd get this pine tar, pine over in the sand hills. They'd heat that and just rub that pine tar all over the inside and outside just like we'd paint ‘em. It's slow work to dig out a canoe.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: I'll bet. Would they have some kind of scrapers or something to help along the progress?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Yes, they did, crude old stuff. No regular scrapers, or anything, crude old stuff. They built several sizes. There were some

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: big old canoes they used to use outside too. I've seen a couple of them. They go between Umpqua and Coos Bay.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Really?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Yes. Big canoes. Carry oh maybe 10 or 12 Indian [?].

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Boy oh boy.

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: 12 canoes. They'd be just about that wide. They'd sit right in the bottom. They kept the canoes real dry. They had these mats. And when they'd pull the canoes up, they'd turn them over and cover them with mats so the sun wouldn't... they'd turn the canoes upside down and always,

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: So they wouldn't check.

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Hmmm, and they always took the paddle up to the house or shack.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: You mean they didn't trust their neighbors?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: I don't know. They always took the paddles up.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: I wonder how they got these logs? Did they just pick up drift logs or would they go in the edge of the forest?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: I couldn't tell you that. I never seen them cut a tree down.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: This has always kind of bothered me.

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: They must have picked them up on the beach, I don't know.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Later on, after the white man came, I understand they had a stage coach from the Winchester Bay or that area, down to opposite Empire here. Do you know where they landed? From Empire, over on the sand hill side?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Well, first, there was a fellow by the name of Hank Barrett. He was a small man.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Barrett?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: ,Hank Barrett. Due east, west of Empire, at that time, there was a big marsh in there. That's where he had his place first. He had his tents in there. He had buildings there - stable and so forth. And the sand just coming and covered up the whole marsh. He got out of there. He went up to Jarvis Landing - started there. He run there quite a while. There was a fellow by the name of Jarvis - Kurt Jarvis bought him out. And he started to run the stage. He ran it for quite a few years., and he was... deputy in something... but he won 15, 000 dollars.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: And he got out of the business.

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Do you recall if there were any provisions for...

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: eee over the stage and run it 'til they discontinued it.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Was thére any provisions for the passengers to stay overnight there in case there was a storm, or the tide was wrong, or anything?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: No, they used be at Empire in the hotel and they'd take them across in the row boat. But then, after they got to .. after while, they quit Empire and went to Marshfield. The steamboat used to take them down. ....They first didn't have any dock there. The row boat would take them right ashore. But then, a guy in the mill company built a dock there. And the steamboats could land.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: In the winter time, that big swale between the sea wall and the timber line would be flooded. Did they have any provisions to across that body of water?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Yes, they had stakes along the - that's to say to signal them where to go and to keep out of the quicksand. It used to be awful crooked, but they had signals there to go by for when it was foggy or something like that. They had stake signals along there.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Do you think of anything Leroy that I haven't...

entries.speaker: Leroy Hanson
entries.text: Herman, about my granddad came in '82. How old were you then? You probably remember when he first came to Haynes Inlet. He bought out from homesteaders didn't he? On Haynes?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: He bought out Benson.

entries.speaker: Leroy Hanson
entries.text: Yeah. Was there more than one? Was there someone else besides Benson?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: I didn't know.

entries.speaker: Leroy Hanson
entries.text: Oh, must not have been.

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Benson was the one that I knew of.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: There's one more question - Where did the Coos Bay bar go out? What did it look like?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Practically same as it is now, only it was about 4 and a half miles wide. There was two, there was center ground - an island in between. Sometimes the north channel would be the deepest, and then it would shift to the south. But the south was principally the channel all the time. And the high water mark - the sea used to come in that bar view ... just the same as it does up at the lighthouse now at. high water. Because it had 4 miles and a half to sweep in there. Boy it'd just fly all over.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Do you recall what Charleston was along in the 1800's?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: What?

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Do you know where Charleston is now?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: Charleston?

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Was there any type of settlement there?

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: In Barview, do you mean?

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: No, across ...

entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: No, that was just the Indians in there.. There was nothing there.

entries.speaker: Dennis Signalness
entries.text: Someone was telling me that there was a Chink, or a Chinaman that had a hotel or something over there, and his name was Charlie. They finally got to calling it Charlie's town of Charleston. Did you ever hear of that.

entries.speaker: Herman Larson

entries.text: In Mr. Peterson's History of Coos and Curry County, he mentions some of the things that the Indians got out of the sand hills for eating and for their household items. entries.speaker: Herman Larson
entries.text: I don't know. But I know they used to get a lot of roots over there. But I don't know the names of them. They roasted something like - well it looked to me something like a squash.
